scope: MAJOR: reverse-reading the ACCEPTED body shows the ps block decodes exactly ONE field (index 0), which finally explains the whole loop
method: ran runs/snapshot-single22.bin (the only accepted body, state 10) with the PsField probe on 0x6701D0 and recorded every field decode
the_model_now: the playerState block is a LOOP; each iteration starts with a has-ps bit, and 0 terminates the block
one iteration decodes exactly ONE field, and the fields are decoded IN ORDER starting at index 0 - the target (V / last_changed+1) is how many fields to reach, not which field to jump to

our accepted body wrote has-ps=1, then V=22, a distance, a 1-bit zero gate, then has-ps=0; so the client decoded ONE field (index 0, codec -97) with value 0 and exited - which is exactly 29 bits: 14 prologue + 13 distance + 1 gate + 1 exit

that also explains the cost growth with V: a larger V makes the decoder want more fields, and it consumes whatever bits follow - so the number of fields it actually reads depends on when it next sees a 0
and it explains why every body that wrote a non-zero value at 'index 22' actually wrote the FIRST field (index 0 = offset 0 = commandTime), which is why those bodies either overran or crashed
consequences: to write a real field such as origin, all the preceding fields in the table (0xDA8520) must be encoded IN ORDER, each with its own codec
the origin-like floats cluster at indices 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16 (codec -88, raw float)
so a coherent body needs indices 0..16 encoded, roughly 17 iterations
